title: Evaluate a Go-to-Market Agent or Prompt Before It Reaches Production
summary: Test a go-to-market agent's prompt in CI before it deploys: a promptfoo suite next to the agent's defineAgent file, run on every pull request that changes either, merged only when it passes. Plus the evaluator that scores each turn in production.
body_markdown:
**To evaluate a go-to-market agent or prompt before it reaches production, keep a[promptfoo](https://www.promptfoo.dev/) suite for it in the same repository as its` defineAgent` file, run` npm run eval` on every pull request that changes either, and make that check required next to Cargo’s own. The prompt deploys only when the merge does, so a failing suite stops it.** Once it is live, the agent’s` evaluator` scores each finished turn against a rubric.


This works because the agent is code. Its system prompt is a string in a TypeScript file, so changing it is a pull request, and a pull request can run tests.


## What the scaffold gives you#


` cargo-ai project init` scaffolds a repository from the open-source[Manifest](https://github.com/getcargohq/cargo-manifest) template, which includes an` evals/` folder:


text


```text
evals/
├── promptfooconfig.yaml   # one provider, prompt and cases per suite
└── _template/
├── prompt.txt         # the agent's prompt, with {{record}} where the input goes
└── cases.yaml         # the four case shapes


```


and a script to run it:


shellscript


```text
npm   run   eval     # runs promptfoo eval -c evals/promptfooconfig.yaml


```


The template’s provider is` openai:gpt-4o` at temperature 0, so it needs` OPENAI_API_KEY` . Set the provider to the model the agent actually runs on, because the suite is only predictive when it approximates the deployed agent.


## Write the suite#


Copy` _template/` to` evals/<agent>/` , paste the agent’s prompt into` prompt.txt` , and fill the four cases the template asks for. They are the four ways a judgment prompt fails:


yaml


```text
# evals/trial-qualifier/cases.yaml
-   description  :   clear fit takes the primary route
vars  :
record  :   "Series B, 120 employees, RevOps team of 3, uses HubSpot"
assert  :
-   type  :   icontains
value  :   "AE"


-   description  :   below the floor is disqualified
vars  :
record  :   "Two-person agency, no CRM"
assert  :
-   type  :   not-icontains
value  :   "AE"


-   description  :   out of profile on the upper edge is not primary-routed
vars  :
record  :   "Public company, 40,000 employees, in-house data platform"
assert  :
-   type  :   not-icontains
value  :   "AE"


-   description  :   missing info takes the safe fallback, no invented facts
vars  :
record  :   "acme.io"
assert  :
-   type  :   icontains
value  :   "nurture"
-   type  :   llm-rubric
value  :   "The response does not invent facts about the record."


```


The third case is the one teams forget: a prompt that only enforces a floor passes oversized accounts. The fourth asserts what a keyword check cannot, that the agent did not make anything up. Add both` file://` lines for the new suite to` promptfooconfig.yaml` .


## Run it on every pull request#


The template ships lint and typecheck workflows, not an eval one, because the suite needs a model API key. Add it:


yaml


```text
# .github/workflows/evals.yml
name  :   evals
on  :
pull_request  :
paths  :
-   "infra/agents/**"
-   "evals/**"
jobs  :
evals  :
runs-on  :   ubuntu-latest
steps  :
-   uses  :   actions/checkout@v4
-   uses  :   actions/setup-node@v4
with  :
node-version  :   22
cache  :   npm
-   run  :   npm ci
-   run  :   npm run eval
env  :
OPENAI_API_KEY  :   ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}


```


Adjust the paths to wherever your agents live. With the repository[connected to Cargo](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/deploy-go-to-market-changes-on-merge) , the same pull request also gets Cargo’s plan check, and the merge is the deploy. Require both checks in branch protection and a prompt that fails its suite cannot reach production. The rule that keeps it honest: when a prompt changes, extend its cases in the same pull request.


## Once it is live: the evaluator#


` defineAgent` takes an` evaluator` , an LLM-as-judge that scores the agent’s output against a rubric:


typescript


```text
export   const   qualifier   =   defineAgent  (  "trial-qualifier"  , {
connector: anthropic,
languageModel:   "claude-sonnet-5"  ,
systemPrompt:   "You qualify trial signups. …"  ,
evaluator: {
rubric:   "Did it correctly qualify the lead, with evidence for the score?"  ,
threshold:   0.8  ,
},
});


```


Cargo scores each finished turn from 0 to 1, with a summary and a pass or fail and a reason for each criterion in the rubric. With a` heartbeat` set, a turn scoring below` threshold` gets another turn with that critique in its prompt. The evaluator is deployed with the agent, so changing the rubric is a reviewed change too.


The two do different jobs. The suite catches a regression before it ships, on cases you wrote. The evaluator catches the cases you did not think of, after it ships.


## What this does not cover#


- Cargo does not run your promptfoo suite for you; it runs in your CI.
- The suite tests the prompt, not the tools the agent calls. A tool that returns bad data passes a prompt test.
- An` llm-rubric` assertion is itself a model call and costs tokens on every run.


For the reasoning behind measuring revenue agents on quality rather than activity, see[LLM evals for revenue agents](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/llm-evals-for-revenue-agents-2026) . The whole lifecycle:[GTM as code: the complete guide](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/gtm-as-code-complete-guide) .
